subject: chemistry
topic: The periodic table: Group 2 (alkaline earth metals)
subtopic: Thermal stability of Group 2 carbonates: cation charge density (polarising power) and the trend down the group
learning_objective: Explain the increase in thermal stability of Group 2 carbonates down the group in terms of decreasing cation charge density and the polarisation of the carbonate anion.
question: The carbonates of the Group 2 metals decompose on heating: MCO3(s) -> MO(s) + CO2(g). Separate samples of magnesium carbonate, calcium carbonate, strontium carbonate and barium carbonate are heated, and the temperature at which each begins to decompose is recorded. Which statement correctly identifies the carbonate that decomposes at the LOWEST temperature, together with a correct reason?

choices.A: Barium carbonate, because the low charge density of the large Ba2+ ion makes its carbonate the least thermally stable.
choices.B: Magnesium carbonate, because the small Mg2+ ion has the highest charge density and most strongly polarises the carbonate ion, weakening a C-O bond.
choices.C: Barium carbonate, because Ba2+ has the greatest polarising power, spreading the same charge over a larger surface.
choices.D: All four decompose at the same temperature, because they contain the same carbonate anion and so have identical decomposition enthalpies.
choices.E: Magnesium carbonate, because the Mg-O bond formed in MgO is the weakest of the four oxides and so forms most readily.

explanation: Down Group 2 the cation radius increases, so charge density (polarising power) decreases: Mg2+ > Ca2+ > Sr2+ > Ba2+. A more polarising cation distorts the electron cloud of the large carbonate anion, weakening a C-O bond and making loss of CO2 easier. Thermal stability therefore increases down the group, so MgCO3 decomposes at the lowest temperature and BaCO3 at the highest.

option_analysis.A: Wrong: identifies the correct governing factor (charge density) but reverses its effect. Low charge density means Ba2+ polarises the anion least, so BaCO3 is the MOST stable and decomposes at the highest temperature, not the lowest.
option_analysis.B: Correct: Mg2+ is the smallest cation and has the highest charge density, so it most strongly polarises the carbonate ion, weakening a C-O bond and giving the lowest decomposition temperature.
option_analysis.C: Wrong: encodes the misconception that a larger ion is more polarising. Polarising power rises with charge density (charge/size); the larger Ba2+ has the LOWEST charge density and the weakest polarising power.
option_analysis.D: Wrong: treats the anion as the sole determinant and ignores the cation. The polarising power of the different cations makes the decomposition temperatures differ markedly across the group.
option_analysis.E: Wrong: chooses the right carbonate but for a spurious reason. Stability is governed by polarisation of the reactant carbonate by the cation, not by the strength of a bond in the product oxide (and MgO in fact has a very high lattice enthalpy).

author: mioitalia_editorial

subject: chemistry
subtopic: Halogen-halide displacement: selective oxidation of the more readily oxidised halide and the colour of the halogen in a non-polar solvent
learning_objective: Apply the trend in reducing power of halide ions down Group 7 to predict which halide is oxidised first by a limited amount of a halogen and the colour observed in a non-polar solvent.
question: An aqueous solution contains potassium bromide and potassium iodide at equal concentrations. Chlorine gas is bubbled slowly into the solution; after only a LIMITED amount of chlorine has been added, the mixture is shaken with a small volume of cyclohexane. Taking the more readily oxidised halide to react first, what is seen in the cyclohexane (upper) layer, and why?

choices.A: An orange layer, because bromide, being the more strongly reducing halide, is oxidised before iodide.
choices.B: A pale green layer, because unreacted chlorine dissolves preferentially in the non-polar solvent.
choices.C: A violet layer, because iodide is the more readily oxidised ion and is displaced first to give iodine.
choices.D: A brown layer coloured throughout both phases, because bromine and iodine are released together in equal amounts.
choices.E: A colourless layer, because chlorine is not able to oxidise either bromide or iodide ions.

explanation: Reducing power of the halide ions increases down Group 7 (I- > Br- > Cl-) because the outer electron is more easily lost from the larger ion. A limited amount of the oxidant, chlorine, therefore oxidises iodide first: Cl2 + 2I- -> 2Cl- + I2. Iodine is violet/purple when dissolved in a non-polar solvent such as cyclohexane (it appears brown in water). Only once all the iodide has reacted would bromide be oxidised to orange bromine.

option_analysis.A: Wrong: reverses the reducing-power order. Bromide is a weaker reducing agent than iodide, so iodide (not bromide) is oxidised first; the orange colour of bromine would appear only later.
option_analysis.B: Wrong: assumes dissolved chlorine colours the organic layer. The limited chlorine is consumed by the halide ions, and chlorine is in any case only faintly coloured; no green colour develops.
option_analysis.C: Correct: iodide is the strongest reducing agent present, so it is oxidised first by the limited chlorine, and the iodine produced gives the characteristic violet colour in cyclohexane.
option_analysis.D: Wrong: ignores the selectivity imposed by a limited amount of oxidant. With chlorine in short supply the more easily oxidised iodide reacts first, so the halogens are not released simultaneously or in equal amounts.
option_analysis.E: Wrong: denies that chlorine can displace the lower halogens. Chlorine is a stronger oxidant than both bromine and iodine and readily oxidises both Br- and I-.

author: mioitalia_editorial

subject: chemistry
topic: The periodic table: Group 2 (alkaline earth metals)
subtopic: Opposing solubility trends of Group 2 hydroxides and sulfates used to separate two Group 2 cations
learning_objective: Use the opposite solubility trends of Group 2 hydroxides (increasing) and sulfates (decreasing) down the group to choose a reagent that selectively precipitates one Group 2 cation.
question: Down Group 2 the hydroxides become MORE soluble in water while the sulfates become LESS soluble. A solution contains magnesium ions and barium ions at similar concentrations. A chemist wants to precipitate essentially all of ONE cation while leaving the other almost entirely in solution. Which single reagent, added in modest excess, gives the cleanest separation, and which ion stays in solution?

choices.A: Add sodium carbonate solution: only magnesium carbonate precipitates while barium carbonate stays dissolved.
choices.B: Add sodium hydroxide solution: barium ions precipitate as Ba(OH)2 and magnesium ions remain in solution.
choices.C: Add dilute sulfuric acid: barium ions precipitate as BaSO4 and magnesium ions remain in solution.
choices.D: Add dilute sulfuric acid: magnesium ions precipitate as MgSO4 and barium ions remain in solution.
choices.E: Add sodium chloride solution: barium chloride precipitates and magnesium chloride remains in solution.

explanation: The two trends run in opposite directions. Hydroxide solubility increases down the group, so Mg(OH)2 is only sparingly soluble while Ba(OH)2 is soluble. Sulfate solubility decreases down the group, so MgSO4 is soluble while BaSO4 is essentially insoluble. Adding sulfate ions therefore precipitates Ba2+ as BaSO4 and leaves Mg2+ in solution. (Adding hydroxide would instead precipitate Mg(OH)2 and leave Ba2+ in solution, but option A states the opposite outcome and is therefore false.)

option_analysis.A: Wrong: assumes selectivity between the carbonates. Both MgCO3 and BaCO3 are insoluble, so carbonate precipitates both cations together and cannot separate them.
option_analysis.B: Wrong: reverses the hydroxide trend. Solubility of the hydroxides increases down the group, so hydroxide precipitates the sparingly soluble Mg(OH)2, not Ba(OH)2; Ba2+ (as soluble Ba(OH)2) would remain in solution.
option_analysis.C: Correct: sulfate solubility decreases down the group, so sulfate precipitates the highly insoluble BaSO4 while the soluble MgSO4 keeps Mg2+ in solution, giving a clean separation.
option_analysis.D: Wrong: reverses the sulfate trend. It is BaSO4, not MgSO4, that is insoluble; MgSO4 is freely soluble and would not precipitate.
option_analysis.E: Wrong: assumes an insoluble Group 2 chloride. Both MgCl2 and BaCl2 are soluble, so adding chloride precipitates neither cation and achieves no separation.

author: mioitalia_editorial

subject: chemistry
topic: The periodic table: Group 2 (alkaline earth metals)
subtopic: Thermal decomposition of Group 2 nitrates: gas-evolution stoichiometry and mass calculation
learning_objective: Combine the decomposition equation of a Group 2 nitrate with the molar gas volume to relate the volume of evolved gas to the mass of nitrate decomposed.
question: Anhydrous barium nitrate is heated until decomposition is complete: 2 Ba(NO3)2(s) -> 2 BaO(s) + 4 NO2(g) + O2(g). The mixture of gases evolved occupies 6.00 dm3 when measured at room temperature and pressure (molar gas volume = 24.0 dm3 mol^-1 at RTP). What mass of barium nitrate decomposed? (Relative atomic masses: N = 14, O = 16, Ba = 137.)
explanation: Total gas amount = 6.00/24.0 = 0.250 mol. The equation shows that 2 mol of Ba(NO3)2 give 4 mol NO2 + 1 mol O2 = 5 mol of gas, i.e. 2.5 mol of gas per mole of nitrate. So n(Ba(NO3)2) = 0.250/2.5 = 0.100 mol. M(Ba(NO3)2) = 137 + 2(14 + 3x16) = 137 + 2(62) = 261 g mol^-1. Mass = 0.100 x 261 = 26.1 g.

option_analysis.A: Wrong (65.3 g): assumes one mole of gas per mole of salt (ignores the reaction stoichiometry), giving n(salt) = 0.250 mol and mass = 0.250 x 261 = 65.3 g.
option_analysis.B: Correct: 0.250 mol gas / 2.5 mol gas per mole of salt = 0.100 mol Ba(NO3)2; multiplied by M = 261 g mol^-1 gives 26.1 g.
option_analysis.C: Wrong (19.9 g): uses the correct 0.100 mol of salt but takes the formula as Ba(NO3) (one nitrate), giving M = 137 + 62 = 199 and 0.100 x 199 = 19.9 g. It misassigns the +2 charge of barium.
option_analysis.D: Wrong (13.1 g): uses the total of 5 mol gas as if it came from 1 mol of salt rather than 2, so n(salt) = 0.250/5 = 0.050 mol and mass = 0.050 x 261 = 13.1 g.
option_analysis.E: Wrong (32.6 g): ignores the oxygen and counts only NO2, taking 2 mol gas per mole of salt, so n(salt) = 0.250/2 = 0.125 mol and mass = 0.125 x 261 = 32.6 g.

author: mioitalia_editorial

subject: chemistry
subtopic: Reactions of solid halides with concentrated sulfuric acid: reducing power of halide ions and the sulfur reduction products down the group
learning_objective: Predict the products of warming solid sodium halides with concentrated sulfuric acid and relate the extent of reduction of sulfur to the increasing reducing power of halide ions down Group 7.
question: Solid sodium chloride, sodium bromide and sodium iodide are each warmed separately with concentrated sulfuric acid. In every case a hydrogen halide is formed at first, but the halide ions differ in how far they can reduce sulfuric acid. Which row correctly gives the ADDITIONAL products of the redox reactions (beyond the hydrogen halide) and reflects the trend in reducing power down Group 7?

choices.A: NaCl: HCl only; NaBr: HBr only; NaI: HI only (no halide reduces the acid).
choices.B: NaCl: no redox (HCl only); NaBr: H2S and Br2; NaI: SO2 and I2.
choices.C: NaCl: Cl2 and H2S; NaBr: Br2 and SO2; NaI: HI only.
choices.D: NaCl: no redox (HCl only); NaBr: SO2 and Br2; NaI: H2S (together with S and I2).
choices.E: NaCl: Cl2 and SO2; NaBr: Br2 and SO2; NaI: I2 and SO2.

explanation: Reducing power of the halide ions increases down the group (I- > Br- > Cl-). Chloride is too weak a reducing agent to reduce sulfuric acid, so only steamy HCl is produced (an acid-base displacement, no change in the +6 oxidation state of sulfur). Bromide is stronger and reduces sulfur from +6 to +4, giving SO2, while itself being oxidised to Br2. Iodide, the strongest reducing agent, reduces sulfur much further - down to -2 in H2S (with some S and SO2 also formed) - and is oxidised to I2. The extent to which sulfuric acid is reduced therefore mirrors the increasing reducing power of the halide ions.

option_analysis.A: Wrong: assumes no halide can reduce sulfuric acid. This ignores the increase in reducing power down the group: bromide and especially iodide do reduce the acid, producing Br2/SO2 and I2/H2S respectively.
option_analysis.B: Wrong: swaps the sulfur products of bromide and iodide, implying bromide reduces the acid further (to H2S) than iodide (to SO2). In reality iodide is the stronger reducing agent and produces H2S, while bromide only reaches SO2.
option_analysis.C: Wrong: reverses the trend, giving the strongest reduction (to H2S) at chloride and none at iodide. Reducing power increases down the group, so the most extensive reduction occurs with iodide, not chloride.
option_analysis.D: Correct: Cl- cannot reduce H2SO4 (HCl only); Br- reduces S from +6 to +4 (SO2) giving Br2; I- reduces S all the way to -2 (H2S), the strongest reduction, giving I2. This matches the reducing-power order I- > Br- > Cl-.
option_analysis.E: Wrong: assumes all three halides behave identically and reduce the acid to SO2. Chloride is in fact too weak to reduce H2SO4, and iodide reduces it beyond SO2 to H2S, so the products are not uniform.

author: mioitalia_editorial

subject: chemistry
subtopic: Thin-layer chromatography on silica (normal phase): Rf calculation, interpretation of adsorption/polarity, and the effect of mobile-phase polarity
learning_objective: Calculate an Rf value and reason from it about the relative polarity and adsorption of components on a polar (silica) stationary phase, and predict how changing the mobile-phase polarity alters Rf.
question: A student analyses a plant extract by thin-layer chromatography on a silica plate (a polar stationary phase) using a non-polar solvent as the mobile phase. After development, the solvent front has risen 8.0 cm from the origin. Two coloured components separate: pigment X is centred 6.0 cm above the origin and pigment Y is centred 2.0 cm above the origin. Which statement is correct?

choices.A: X has an Rf of 0.75 and is less polar than Y.
choices.B: X has an Rf of 0.75 and is more strongly adsorbed to the silica than Y.
choices.C: If a more polar solvent were used as the mobile phase, both pigments would move with smaller Rf values.
choices.D: Y has an Rf of 0.25 and is less polar than X.
choices.E: X has an Rf of 1.3, obtained by dividing the distance moved by the solvent front by the distance moved by the pigment.

explanation: Rf = (distance moved by the component)/(distance moved by the solvent front). Rf(X) = 6.0/8.0 = 0.75 and Rf(Y) = 2.0/8.0 = 0.25. On silica (a polar stationary phase), a component that is more polar is more strongly adsorbed and is held back, giving a LOW Rf; a less polar component interacts weakly with the plate, is carried further by the non-polar solvent, and has a HIGH Rf. X (Rf 0.75) has travelled further, so it is the less strongly adsorbed, less polar pigment; Y (Rf 0.25) is the more polar, more retained pigment. Increasing the polarity of the mobile phase on a normal-phase (silica) plate increases the eluting strength, so spots move further and Rf values rise, not fall.

option_analysis.A: Correct: Rf(X) = 6.0/8.0 = 0.75; X migrates further with the non-polar solvent because it is only weakly adsorbed to the polar silica, so X is the less polar pigment while the strongly retained Y is more polar.
option_analysis.B: Wrong: Rf(X) = 0.75 is correct, but a higher Rf means the component travelled further, i.e. it is LESS strongly adsorbed to the polar plate, not more. Misconception: treating greater migration as evidence of stronger attraction to the stationary phase.
option_analysis.C: Wrong: on a polar (normal-phase) silica plate a more polar mobile phase has greater eluting power, so components move further and Rf values increase. Misconception: assuming a more polar solvent always lowers Rf, which is the behaviour of reversed-phase, not silica, plates.
option_analysis.D: Wrong: Rf(Y) = 0.25 is correct, but because Y is strongly retained on the polar silica it must be MORE polar than X, not less. Misconception: reversing the retention-polarity relationship on a normal-phase plate.
option_analysis.E: Wrong: the Rf ratio is inverted here (8.0/6.0 = 1.3). Rf is component distance over solvent-front distance and can never exceed 1. Misconception: swapping numerator and denominator in the Rf definition.

author: mioitalia_editorial

subject: chemistry
subtopic: Simple versus fractional distillation of miscible liquids: vapour composition, when a fractionating column is needed, and distinguishing close boiling points from an azeotrope
learning_objective: Reason from boiling points and vapour composition to decide whether simple or fractional distillation is appropriate and to predict the composition of the first distillate.
question: Two completely miscible liquids A and B have boiling points of 78 degrees C and 82 degrees C respectively and do not form an azeotrope. A student gently heats the mixture and collects the first few cubic centimetres of distillate using a simple distillation apparatus (no fractionating column). Which statement about this first distillate is correct?

choices.A: It is pure A, because A boils first at 78 degrees C and only A is present in the vapour.
choices.B: It is richer in B than the original mixture, because B is less volatile and therefore accumulates preferentially in the vapour.
choices.C: It is richer in A than the original mixture, and a fractionating column would be needed to obtain essentially pure A.
choices.D: The liquids cannot be separated by any form of distillation, because a boiling-point difference of only 4 degrees C means they behave as an azeotrope.
choices.E: It is pure B, because the higher-boiling liquid condenses first when the vapour reaches the condenser.

explanation: The vapour in equilibrium with a boiling mixture of two miscible liquids is always enriched in the MORE volatile (lower-boiling) component, here A, but it is not pure: it still contains some B. A single vaporisation-condensation step (simple distillation) therefore gives a distillate richer in A than the starting mixture, not pure A, especially when the boiling points are close (only 4 degrees C apart). To obtain essentially pure A the vapour must undergo many successive vaporisation-condensation cycles, which is exactly what a fractionating column provides (fractional distillation). A small boiling-point difference does not create an azeotrope; provided no azeotrope forms (as stated), fractional distillation can fully separate the pair.

option_analysis.A: Wrong: the vapour is enriched in A but is not pure A; B is volatile too and appears in the vapour. Misconception: believing the lower-boiling component distils over completely pure in a single simple-distillation step.
option_analysis.B: Wrong: the vapour is enriched in the MORE volatile component (A), not the less volatile B. Misconception: assuming the less volatile liquid concentrates in the vapour phase.
option_analysis.C: Correct: the equilibrium vapour is enriched in the more volatile A, so the first distillate is richer in A than the mixture; because the boiling points are close, one simple step is insufficient and a fractionating column (fractional distillation) is required to reach essentially pure A.
option_analysis.D: Wrong: a 4 degrees C difference is small but the question states no azeotrope forms, so fractional distillation still separates them. Misconception: equating any small boiling-point gap with an azeotrope.
option_analysis.E: Wrong: this reverses the volatility relationship. The vapour is richer in the more volatile (lower-boiling) A, and condensation order does not favour the higher-boiling liquid. Misconception: thinking the higher-boiling component comes over first.

author: mioitalia_editorial

subject: chemistry
subtopic: Liquid-liquid solvent extraction: partition (distribution) coefficient and why several small portions extract more than one large portion
learning_objective: Apply the partition coefficient to compute the fraction of solute remaining after single and repeated extractions and show that dividing the extracting solvent into smaller portions improves the extraction.
question: A solute S is dissolved in 100 cm^3 of water. S partitions between diethyl ether and water with a distribution coefficient K = (concentration of S in ether)/(concentration of S in water) = 4.0; the two solvents are immiscible. The aqueous solution is extracted with ether in two successive portions of 50 cm^3 each, the ether layer being removed between the two extractions. What fraction of the original S remains in the aqueous layer after the second extraction?
explanation: For each extraction the fraction of solute remaining in water is f = V(water) / [V(water) + K x V(ether)]. For one 50 cm^3 portion, f = 100 / (100 + 4.0 x 50) = 100/300 = 1/3. Because each extraction acts on what is left, two successive 50 cm^3 portions leave (1/3) x (1/3) = 1/9 of S in the water. (A single 100 cm^3 extraction would leave 100/(100 + 4.0 x 100) = 1/5, which is more than 1/9, so splitting the solvent into two portions extracts more efficiently.)

option_analysis.A: Wrong: 1/3 is the fraction remaining after only ONE 50 cm^3 extraction. Misconception: forgetting to apply the second extraction to the residue.
option_analysis.B: Wrong: 1/5 is the fraction left after a SINGLE 100 cm^3 extraction, treating the two 50 cm^3 portions as one 100 cm^3 step. Misconception: assuming that how the solvent is divided makes no difference to the amount extracted.
option_analysis.C: Correct: each 50 cm^3 portion leaves 100/(100 + 4.0 x 50) = 1/3, so two successive portions leave (1/3)^2 = 1/9 of S in the aqueous layer.
option_analysis.D: Wrong: 4/9 = (2/3)^2 squares the fraction EXTRACTED per step (2/3) rather than the fraction remaining (1/3). Misconception: confusing the fraction removed with the fraction left behind.
option_analysis.E: Wrong: 1/25 = (1/5)^2 squares the single-100 cm^3 fraction, i.e. it wrongly uses 100 cm^3 of ether in each of the two steps. Misconception: using the full solvent volume per step yet still squaring for two extractions.

author: mioitalia_editorial

subject: chemistry
subtopic: Recrystallisation of an impure organic solid: minimum hot solvent, loss to the cold mother liquor from the solid's low-temperature solubility, and impurity remaining in solution
learning_objective: Combine the concept of minimum hot solvent with temperature-dependent solubility to calculate the maximum mass of pure solid recoverable by a single recrystallisation, accounting for material lost in the mother liquor and for the soluble impurity.
question: A 10.0 g sample of an impure organic solid contains 9.0 g of compound C and 1.0 g of a coloured impurity that is very soluble in the chosen solvent. In this solvent, C has a solubility of 90 g per 100 cm^3 at 80 degrees C and 10 g per 100 cm^3 at 10 degrees C. The 9.0 g of C is dissolved in the minimum volume of solvent at 80 degrees C, the solution is filtered hot, then cooled to 10 degrees C and the crystals are collected. Assuming the impurity remains entirely in solution, what is the maximum mass of pure C that can be recovered in this single recrystallisation?
explanation: The minimum volume of hot solvent just dissolves the 9.0 g of C at 80 degrees C, where the solubility is 90 g per 100 cm^3: volume = (9.0/90) x 100 = 10 cm^3. On cooling this same 10 cm^3 to 10 degrees C, the solvent can still hold C up to its low-temperature solubility of 10 g per 100 cm^3, i.e. 10 cm^3 retains (10/100) x 10 = 1.0 g of C dissolved in the mother liquor. The mass of C that crystallises out is therefore 9.0 - 1.0 = 8.0 g. The 1.0 g of impurity stays in solution (it is well below its own saturation), so it is removed in the mother liquor and the recovered crystals are pure. Maximum recovery of pure C = 8.0 g.

option_analysis.A: Wrong: 8.1 g comes from taking the 10 degrees C solubility as 10 percent of the DISSOLVED SOLUTE mass (0.10 x 9.0 = 0.9 g lost). Solubility is a mass per unit VOLUME of solvent (1.0 g in 10 cm^3), not a percentage of the solute. Misconception: applying solubility as a fraction of the solute rather than per volume of solvent.
option_analysis.B: Wrong: 7.0 g subtracts both the 1.0 g of C left in the mother liquor and the 1.0 g of impurity from 9.0 g. The impurity is not part of C, so it should not be deducted from the recoverable C mass. Misconception: double-counting the impurity as a loss of product.
option_analysis.C: Correct: minimum hot solvent = 10 cm^3; at 10 degrees C that volume retains 1.0 g of C in solution, so 9.0 - 1.0 = 8.0 g of pure C crystallises while the soluble impurity stays in the mother liquor.
option_analysis.D: Wrong: 10.0 g is the whole original sample, including the 1.0 g impurity and assuming zero solubility loss. Recrystallisation deliberately leaves the impurity (and some C) in the mother liquor and never recovers 100 percent. Misconception: assuming recrystallisation gives complete mass recovery and does not discard the impurity.
option_analysis.E: Wrong: 9.0 g assumes every gram of C crystallises on cooling, ignoring that C still has an appreciable solubility (10 g per 100 cm^3) at 10 degrees C so 1.0 g stays dissolved. Misconception: treating cooling as recovering 100 percent of the dissolved solute.

author: mioitalia_editorial

subject: chemistry
subtopic: The greenhouse effect: infrared absorption requires a change in dipole moment (why CO2 is IR-active but N2, O2 and Ar are not)
learning_objective: Explain that a gas absorbs infrared radiation (and hence acts as a greenhouse gas) only if a molecular vibration changes its dipole moment, distinguishing this requirement from the presence of a permanent dipole.
question: The four most abundant gases in dry air are nitrogen (N2, about 78%), oxygen (O2, about 21%), argon (Ar, about 0.9%) and carbon dioxide (CO2, about 0.04%). Although it is present only in trace amounts, carbon dioxide makes a significant contribution to the greenhouse effect, whereas the far more abundant N2, O2 and Ar do not. Which statement gives the correct reason?

choices.A: A molecule absorbs infrared radiation only if one of its vibrations changes the molecule's dipole moment; the bending and asymmetric-stretching vibrations of carbon dioxide do this, whereas the single vibration of N2 or O2 produces no change in dipole and argon (a single atom) cannot vibrate at all.
choices.B: N2 and O2 cannot absorb infrared radiation because the bonds between two identical atoms are too strong to vibrate, whereas the polar C=O bonds in carbon dioxide vibrate readily.
choices.C: Only gases denser than air, such as carbon dioxide, can trap outgoing infrared radiation close to the ground, whereas the lighter N2 and O2 rise above the emitted radiation.
choices.D: Carbon dioxide is a greenhouse gas because it is a polar molecule with a permanent dipole moment, whereas N2, O2 and Ar are non-polar.
choices.E: Carbon dioxide absorbs infrared radiation because the photons promote its electrons to higher energy levels, while the electrons in N2 and O2 are held too tightly to be excited.

explanation: Infrared photons carry the right amount of energy to excite molecular vibrations (bond stretching and bending), not electronic transitions. A vibration can absorb an IR photon only if it produces an oscillating (changing) dipole moment that the electromagnetic wave can couple to. A homonuclear diatomic such as N2 or O2 has a single vibrational mode (the stretch); because the two atoms are identical, the dipole moment stays zero throughout the vibration, so the mode is IR-inactive. Argon is monatomic and has no vibration at all. Carbon dioxide is linear and symmetric, so it has NO permanent dipole moment, yet its bending mode and its asymmetric stretch generate a temporary oscillating dipole and are therefore IR-active. This is why a trace of a symmetric, non-polar molecule such as CO2 can still be a potent greenhouse gas: the key requirement is a change in dipole moment during vibration, not a permanent dipole.

option_analysis.A: Correct: IR absorption requires a vibration that changes the dipole moment. CO2's bending and asymmetric-stretch modes satisfy this despite its zero permanent dipole, while the single mode of homonuclear N2/O2 does not, and monatomic argon has no vibration.
option_analysis.B: Wrong: bond strength is not the reason. N2 and O2 do vibrate; their stretching vibration is simply IR-inactive because it produces no change in dipole moment. This confuses vibrational activity with bond dissociation.
option_analysis.C: Wrong: molar mass and density are irrelevant to infrared absorption. Gases mix throughout the atmosphere by diffusion and convection; this option invents a 'settling' mechanism that does not exist.
option_analysis.D: Wrong: encodes the common misconception that a greenhouse gas must have a permanent dipole. Carbon dioxide is linear and symmetric and has a net dipole moment of zero, yet it is a greenhouse gas, so a permanent dipole is not the criterion.
option_analysis.E: Wrong: it confuses infrared (vibrational) absorption with electronic excitation. Promoting electrons to higher levels requires the much higher energies of ultraviolet/visible photons; IR absorption by greenhouse gases is vibrational.

author: mioitalia_editorial

subject: chemistry
subtopic: Stratospheric ozone depletion: photolytic initiation of CFCs — preferential cleavage of the weaker C–Cl bond and tropospheric persistence
learning_objective: Account for the ozone-depleting action of CFCs by combining bond-enthalpy data (preferential C–Cl cleavage), tropospheric inertness and the catalytic nature of the chlorine atoms released.
question: Chlorofluorocarbons (CFCs) such as dichlorodifluoromethane, CCl2F2, were once widely used as refrigerants and are now known to deplete stratospheric ozone. Relevant mean bond enthalpies are: C–F 485 kJ mol^-1, C–Cl 327 kJ mol^-1, C–H 413 kJ mol^-1. Which statement best accounts for the behaviour of CFCs in the atmosphere?

choices.A: In the stratosphere, ultraviolet light cleaves the strongest bond present, the C–F bond, releasing fluorine atoms that are the true catalysts of ozone destruction.
choices.B: CFCs deplete ozone because they are greenhouse gases: they warm the stratosphere, and the higher temperature decomposes ozone thermally.
choices.C: Because they are chemically inert, CFCs persist long enough to diffuse up into the stratosphere, where ultraviolet light preferentially cleaves the weaker C–Cl bond to release chlorine atoms, which then catalyse the breakdown of ozone.
choices.D: CFCs are so reactive that they begin destroying ozone as soon as they are released at ground level; their low boiling points merely help them disperse.
choices.E: Each chlorine atom is consumed stoichiometrically, so one CFC molecule can destroy at most a number of ozone molecules equal to the number of chlorine atoms it contains.

explanation: CFCs owe their environmental impact to a combination of three ideas. (1) In the troposphere they are extremely unreactive (no O–H to abstract, not attacked by water or oxidants), so instead of being destroyed near the surface they survive for decades and slowly mix upward into the stratosphere. (2) There, high-energy (short-wavelength) ultraviolet light is available and photodissociation breaks the weakest bond first. Comparing the bond enthalpies, C–Cl (327 kJ mol^-1) is much weaker than C–F (485 kJ mol^-1), so a chlorine atom (a free radical, Cl-) is released rather than a fluorine atom. (3) The chlorine atom then acts as a catalyst: it is regenerated in the propagation cycle, so a single atom destroys many thousands of ozone molecules before it is finally removed as a reservoir species. Option B captures all three points correctly.

option_analysis.A: Wrong: photolysis breaks the WEAKEST bond, not the strongest; the C–F bond (485 kJ mol^-1) is the hardest to break. It also wrongly names fluorine as the catalyst, whereas chlorine atoms drive the destruction.
option_analysis.B: Wrong: it conflates the greenhouse (infrared-trapping) role of CFCs with ozone chemistry. Ozone destruction here is a photochemical, catalytic free-radical process, not thermal decomposition driven by warming.
option_analysis.C: Correct: tropospheric inertness gives them the lifetime to reach the stratosphere, UV cleaves the weaker C–Cl bond (327 < 485 kJ mol^-1) to give Cl atoms, and these catalyse ozone loss.
option_analysis.D: Wrong: this reverses the truth. CFCs are valued precisely because they are inert and non-flammable; their lack of reactivity in the troposphere is what allows them to reach the stratosphere. Reactivity at ground level is the misconception.
option_analysis.E: Wrong: it treats chlorine as being used up stoichiometrically. In fact the chlorine atom is a catalyst, regenerated each cycle, so one atom destroys of the order of 10^5 ozone molecules, far more than the two chlorines in the parent molecule.

author: mioitalia_editorial

subject: chemistry
subtopic: Acid rain from SO2: flue-gas desulfurisation with limestone — stoichiometric mass of CaCO3 needed to remove sulfur dioxide
learning_objective: Apply reacting-mass stoichiometry to flue-gas desulfurisation, calculating the mass of calcium carbonate needed to remove the sulfur dioxide produced when a sulfur-containing fuel is burned.
question: A power station burns 1.0 tonne (1.0 x 10^3 kg) of coal containing 2.0% sulfur by mass. On combustion all of the sulfur is converted to sulfur dioxide, which would otherwise form sulfuric acid in rain. The sulfur dioxide is instead completely removed by reaction with powdered calcium carbonate in a scrubber: CaCO3 + SO2 -> CaSO3 + CO2. What mass of calcium carbonate is required? (Relative atomic masses: S 32, Ca 40, C 12, O 16.)
explanation: First find the mass of sulfur: 2.0% of 1.0 x 10^6 g = 2.0 x 10^4 g = 20 kg. Each sulfur atom becomes one SO2 molecule, so moles of SO2 = moles of S = 20000 g / 32 g mol^-1 = 625 mol. The scrubbing reaction is 1:1 in SO2 and CaCO3, so 625 mol of CaCO3 is needed. The molar mass of CaCO3 is 40 + 12 + (3 x 16) = 100 g mol^-1, giving a mass of 625 x 100 = 62500 g = 62.5 kg. The clean chain is: mass S -> mol S = mol SO2 = mol CaCO3 -> mass CaCO3.

option_analysis.A: Correct: 625 mol of SO2 requires 625 mol of CaCO3 (1:1), and 625 x 100 = 62500 g = 62.5 kg.
option_analysis.B: Wrong: 25 kg = 625 mol x 40 g mol^-1. This uses the relative atomic mass of calcium (40) instead of the molar mass of the whole formula unit CaCO3 (100), a formula-mass error.
option_analysis.C: Wrong: 125 kg = 2 x 62.5 kg. This assumes a 2:1 ratio of CaCO3 to SO2, misreading the balanced equation, which is 1:1.
option_analysis.D: Wrong: 20 kg is simply the mass of sulfur in the coal. It omits the whole mole-to-mass conversion, treating the mass of sulfur as if it were the mass of calcium carbonate.
option_analysis.E: Wrong: 31.25 kg = (20000/64) x 100. This divides the sulfur mass by the molar mass of SO2 (64) rather than by the atomic mass of S (32) to get the moles, wrongly using the compound mass with the element mass.

author: mioitalia_editorial

subject: chemistry
subtopic: Catalytic converters: the 2CO + 2NO -> 2CO2 + N2 redox reaction — oxidation-state changes, oxidising/reducing agents and heterogeneous catalysis
learning_objective: Analyse the catalytic-converter reaction 2CO + 2NO -> 2CO2 + N2 in terms of oxidation-number changes, the identity of the oxidising and reducing agents, and the role of a heterogeneous catalyst.
question: A three-way catalytic converter in a car's exhaust system promotes, among others, the reaction: 2 CO(g) + 2 NO(g) -> 2 CO2(g) + N2(g). Which statement about this reaction is correct?

choices.A: Nitrogen is oxidised from +2 to 0 and carbon is reduced from +2 to +4, so nitrogen monoxide is the reducing agent.
choices.B: Both carbon and nitrogen are oxidised in this reaction, which is why two different reducing agents (CO and NO) are required.
choices.C: This is an acid-base neutralisation in which carbon monoxide, a basic oxide, reacts with nitrogen monoxide, an acidic oxide.
choices.D: Carbon is oxidised from +2 to +4 and nitrogen is reduced from +2 to 0; carbon monoxide is the reducing agent and nitrogen monoxide is the oxidising agent.
choices.E: The platinum catalyst is oxidised by NO and then reduced by CO, so it is gradually consumed and must be replaced regularly.

explanation: Assign oxidation numbers using O = -2. In CO, carbon is +2; in CO2 it is +4, so carbon is OXIDISED (+2 -> +4, loses electrons), which makes CO the reducing agent. In NO, nitrogen is +2; in N2 it is 0, so nitrogen is REDUCED (+2 -> 0, gains electrons), which makes NO the oxidising agent. The converter thus simultaneously oxidises the pollutant CO (and unburnt hydrocarbons) and reduces the pollutant NO to harmless N2. The transition-metal coating (Pt/Pd/Rh) is a heterogeneous catalyst: the gases adsorb, react on its surface and desorb, and the catalyst is regenerated, not consumed.

option_analysis.A: Wrong: it reverses both changes. Going from +2 to 0 is a decrease in oxidation number (reduction, not oxidation), and +2 to +4 is an increase (oxidation, not reduction). It therefore also misassigns NO as the reducing agent.
option_analysis.B: Wrong: in any redox reaction electrons transferred by an oxidation must be gained by a reduction; both species cannot be oxidised. Here nitrogen is reduced, so 'both oxidised' is impossible.
option_analysis.C: Wrong: this is a redox process, not an acid-base neutralisation. CO and NO are neutral oxides here undergoing electron transfer, and no salt or water is formed.
option_analysis.D: Correct: C goes +2 -> +4 (oxidised, CO is the reducing agent) and N goes +2 -> 0 (reduced, NO is the oxidising agent), which is exactly what the converter must achieve.
option_analysis.E: Wrong: a catalyst is not consumed. The metal provides a surface on which the reaction proceeds and is regenerated each cycle; the misconception is that the catalyst is a reactant used up in the process.

author: mioitalia_editorial

subject: chemistry
subtopic: Stratospheric ozone depletion: the ClO/Cl free-radical propagation cycle — net reaction, catalyst versus intermediate and catalytic turnover
learning_objective: Interpret the chlorine free-radical chain that destroys stratospheric ozone: derive the net reaction, distinguish the catalyst from the reaction intermediate, and quantify catalytic turnover.
question: In the stratosphere a chlorine atom destroys ozone through the repeating two-step cycle: Step 1: Cl- + O3 -> ClO- + O2; Step 2: ClO- + O- -> Cl- + O2. The oxygen atoms (O-) are supplied by the ultraviolet photodissociation of O2 and O3. On average a chlorine atom completes 1.0 x 10^5 of these cycles before it is removed by conversion into a stable 'reservoir' molecule. Considering a single chlorine atom, which statement is correct?

choices.A: The net reaction is O3 + O- -> 2 O2; ClO- is the catalyst because it is regenerated each cycle, and about 1 x 10^5 ozone molecules are destroyed.
choices.B: Because each cycle also consumes an oxygen atom that would otherwise have formed ozone, about 2 x 10^5 ozone molecules are removed, and ClO- is the catalyst.
choices.C: The net reaction is O3 + O- -> 2 O2; Cl- is the catalyst (regenerated each cycle) and ClO- is a reaction intermediate, and about 1 x 10^5 ozone molecules are destroyed by one chlorine atom.
choices.D: The net reaction is O3 + O- -> 2 O2; Cl- is consumed permanently in the cycle, so only one ozone molecule is destroyed per chlorine atom.
choices.E: The net reaction is 2 O3 -> 3 O2; Cl- is the reaction intermediate and ClO- is the catalyst, and about 2 x 10^5 ozone molecules are destroyed.

explanation: Add the two propagation steps and cancel species that appear on both sides. Cl- + O3 + ClO- + O- -> ClO- + O2 + Cl- + O2. Both Cl- and ClO- cancel, leaving the net reaction O3 + O- -> 2 O2. The species Cl- is consumed in Step 1 but regenerated in Step 2, so it is the CATALYST; ClO- is produced in Step 1 and consumed in Step 2, so it is a reaction INTERMEDIATE. Because Cl- is regenerated, a single atom cycles repeatedly. Only Step 1 destroys an ozone molecule (one O3 per cycle; Step 2 consumes an oxygen atom, not O3), so 1.0 x 10^5 cycles destroy about 1.0 x 10^5 ozone molecules. Option E states all of this correctly.

option_analysis.A: Wrong: the net reaction and the count (10^5) are right, but it identifies the catalyst incorrectly. The species regenerated each cycle is Cl-, whereas ClO- is formed and then consumed, making ClO- the intermediate, not the catalyst.
option_analysis.B: Wrong: only one O3 is destroyed per cycle (in Step 1); the oxygen atom removed in Step 2 is not an ozone molecule, so the count is 1 x 10^5, not 2 x 10^5. It also misidentifies ClO- as the catalyst.
option_analysis.C: Correct: the steps sum to O3 + O- -> 2 O2, Cl- is regenerated (catalyst) while ClO- is the intermediate, and with one O3 destroyed per cycle, 1.0 x 10^5 cycles remove about 1.0 x 10^5 ozone molecules.
option_analysis.D: Wrong: it treats Cl- as being permanently consumed, which contradicts Step 2 that regenerates it. Because Cl- is a catalyst, one atom destroys of the order of 10^5 ozone molecules, not one.
option_analysis.E: Wrong on three counts: the net reaction of the catalytic cycle is O3 + O- -> 2 O2, not 2 O3 -> 3 O2 (that is the uncatalysed ozone decomposition); it swaps the roles of catalyst and intermediate; and it doubles the ozone count.

author: mioitalia_editorial

subject: chemistry
subtopic: Calorimetry of an exothermic metal-displacement reaction: molar enthalpy change from q = mcΔT with a limiting-reactant step
learning_objective: Calculate a molar reaction enthalpy from calorimetric data using q = mcΔT, correctly identifying the limiting reactant as the basis for the per-mole conversion and assigning the sign from the temperature change.
question: A student adds an excess of zinc powder to 50.0 cm3 of 0.200 mol dm-3 copper(II) sulfate solution in an insulated cup and stirs. The temperature of the solution rises from 21.0 C to 31.0 C. Assume the solution has the density and specific heat capacity of water (1.00 g cm-3; 4.18 J g-1 C-1) and that the zinc contributes negligibly to the heat capacity. What is the molar enthalpy change for the reaction Zn(s) + Cu2+(aq) -> Zn2+(aq) + Cu(s)?
explanation: In calorimetry the heat gained by the solution equals the heat released by the reaction, and q = mcDT uses the mass of the SOLUTION, not of the reactant. Convert to a molar quantity by dividing by the moles of the limiting reactant: zinc is in excess, so Cu2+ is limiting, n(Cu2+) = 0.0500 dm3 x 0.200 mol dm-3 = 0.0100 mol. q = 50.0 x 4.18 x 10.0 = 2090 J. Because the temperature rises, the surroundings gained heat and the system lost it, so DH is negative: DH = -q/n = -2090/0.0100 = -2.09x10^5 J mol-1 = -209 kJ mol-1.

option_analysis.A: Wrong: divides by 0.00500 mol, i.e. uses half the amount of Cu2+ (as if only 25.0 cm3 had been taken). Halving the moles doubles the apparent molar enthalpy.
option_analysis.B: Wrong: correct magnitude but positive sign. A temperature rise shows heat is released to the solution, so the reaction is exothermic and DH must be negative (sign-convention error).
option_analysis.C: Wrong: this is simply the heat released, q = 2.09 kJ, quoted without dividing by the number of moles; it is not a molar (per-mole) quantity.
option_analysis.D: Wrong: divides q (2090 J) by 0.200 rather than by the amount in moles, i.e. treats the concentration (0.200 mol dm-3) as if it were the number of moles of Cu2+.
option_analysis.E: Correct: q = mcDT = 50.0 x 4.18 x 10.0 = 2090 J; the limiting Cu2+ is 0.0500 dm3 x 0.200 mol dm-3 = 0.0100 mol; DH = -2090/0.0100 = -209 kJ mol-1 (exothermic).

author: mioitalia_editorial

subject: chemistry
subtopic: Enthalpy of neutralisation from calorimetry with a diprotic acid: moles of water formed and the total-mass trap
learning_objective: Determine an enthalpy of neutralisation per mole of water from calorimetric data, accounting for the diprotic nature of the acid and using the combined mass of the mixed solutions.
question: 25.0 cm3 of 1.00 mol dm-3 sulfuric acid at 21.0 C is mixed with 50.0 cm3 of 1.00 mol dm-3 sodium hydroxide at 21.0 C in an insulated cup. The temperature rises to a maximum of 30.1 C. Assume every solution has the density and specific heat capacity of water (1.00 g cm-3; 4.18 J g-1 C-1). What is the enthalpy of neutralisation (per mole of water formed)?
explanation: Enthalpy of neutralisation is defined per mole of water formed. Sulfuric acid is diprotic: 0.0250 mol H2SO4 supplies 2 x 0.0250 = 0.0500 mol H+, which exactly neutralises 0.0500 mol OH-, so 0.0500 mol of water forms (neither reagent is in excess). The heat is absorbed by the whole mixture, of combined mass 25.0 + 50.0 = 75.0 g, over DT = 9.1 C: q = 75.0 x 4.18 x 9.1 = 2850 J = 2.85 kJ. DH = -q/n(H2O) = -2.85/0.0500 = -57.1 kJ mol-1; the temperature rises, so neutralisation is exothermic and the sign is negative.

option_analysis.A: Correct: n(H+) = 2 x 0.0250 = 0.0500 mol matches 0.0500 mol OH-, giving 0.0500 mol water; using the combined 75.0 g, q = 75.0 x 4.18 x 9.1 = 2.85 kJ, so DH = -2.85/0.0500 = -57.1 kJ mol-1.
option_analysis.B: Wrong: treats sulfuric acid as monoprotic, taking only 0.0250 mol H+ (hence 0.0250 mol water). Being diprotic, H2SO4 supplies 2 mol H+ per mole, so 0.0500 mol water forms.
option_analysis.C: Wrong: correct magnitude but wrong sign; the temperature rises, so neutralisation is exothermic and DH must be negative.
option_analysis.D: Wrong: divides the heat by the total amount of the two reagents (0.0250 mol H2SO4 + 0.0500 mol NaOH = 0.0750 mol) instead of by the moles of water formed.
option_analysis.E: Wrong: uses only 25.0 g (the acid volume) as the mass of solution rather than the combined 75.0 g, making q one-third of the true value.

author: mioitalia_editorial

subject: chemistry
subtopic: Enthalpy of combustion by calorimetry: molar value from the calorimeter heat capacity with a sample-purity correction
learning_objective: Calculate a standard molar enthalpy of combustion from a calorimeter heat-capacity measurement, applying a purity correction to the burned mass and converting to a per-mole basis with the correct sign.
question: A 1.00 g sample of impure glucose (C6H12O6, M = 180 g mol-1) that is 90.0% glucose by mass, the remaining 10.0% being an inert non-combustible solid, is burned completely in a calorimeter whose total heat capacity is 10.0 kJ K-1. The temperature of the calorimeter rises by 1.40 K. What is the standard molar enthalpy of combustion of glucose?
explanation: The heat released is obtained from the calorimeter's heat capacity, not from q = mcDT of water: q = C x DT = 10.0 kJ K-1 x 1.40 K = 14.0 kJ. Only the glucose burns, and the purity correction is applied to the MASS: glucose = 0.900 x 1.00 g = 0.900 g, so n = 0.900/180 = 0.00500 mol. Combustion is exothermic (temperature rises), so DH = -q/n = -14.0/0.00500 = -2800 kJ mol-1.

option_analysis.A: Wrong: uses the whole 1.00 g sample (1.00/180 = 0.00556 mol) and ignores that only 90.0% is glucose, so the amount is overstated.
option_analysis.C: Wrong: uses an incorrect molar mass of 90 g mol-1 (0.900/90 = 0.0100 mol), doubling the amount and halving the magnitude.
option_analysis.D: Wrong: correct magnitude but positive sign; combustion releases heat (temperature rises), so DH is negative.
option_analysis.E: Wrong: obtains -2800 then divides again by the purity fraction 0.90. The purity correction belongs on the mass of glucose, not on the final enthalpy value.

author: mioitalia_editorial

subject: chemistry
subtopic: Standard enthalpy of formation of a hydrocarbon from enthalpies of combustion (Hess cycle)
learning_objective: Apply Hess's law to obtain a compound's standard enthalpy of formation from the standard enthalpies of combustion of its elements and of the compound, using the correct stoichiometric coefficients and cycle direction.
question: Use the following standard enthalpies of combustion: C(graphite) -394 kJ mol-1; H2(g) -286 kJ mol-1; propane C3H8(g) -2220 kJ mol-1. What is the standard enthalpy of formation of propane, DHf[C3H8(g)]?
explanation: Both the elements (3C + 4H2) and propane burn to the same products (3CO2 + 4H2O). By Hess's law, going 'elements -> products' directly equals 'elements -> propane -> products': DHf(propane) + DHc(propane) = sum of DHc(elements). Therefore DHf = [3 x DHc(C) + 4 x DHc(H2)] - DHc(propane). Propane has 8 H atoms, so 4 mol H2 are needed. DHf = [3(-394) + 4(-286)] - (-2220) = (-1182 - 1144) + 2220 = -2326 + 2220 = -106 kJ mol-1.

option_analysis.A: Wrong: uses only 3 mol H2 (as if C3H8 -> 3C + 3H2). Propane contains 8 H atoms, i.e. 4 mol H2: 3(-394) + 3(-286) - (-2220) = +180.
option_analysis.C: Wrong: adds the combustion enthalpy of propane instead of subtracting it: 3(-394) + 4(-286) + (-2220) = -4546. The compound term must be reversed in the cycle.
option_analysis.D: Wrong: sums the combustion enthalpies of the elements (3(-394) + 4(-286) = -2326) but forgets to subtract the combustion enthalpy of propane.
option_analysis.E: Wrong: correct magnitude but wrong sign; the whole cycle has been run in reverse, giving DHc(propane) - sum of DHc(elements).

author: mioitalia_editorial

subject: chemistry
subtopic: Estimating the enthalpy of combustion of an alkene from average bond enthalpies (multiple bond types, gaseous products)
learning_objective: Estimate a reaction enthalpy from average bond enthalpies by correctly enumerating every bond broken and formed in a balanced equation (including double bonds and multiple identical bonds) and applying DH = (bonds broken) - (bonds formed).
question: Estimate the enthalpy change for the complete combustion of ethene, producing gaseous water: C2H4(g) + 3 O2(g) -> 2 CO2(g) + 2 H2O(g). Use the average bond enthalpies (kJ mol-1): C=C 612; C-H 412; O=O 496; C=O (in CO2) 805; O-H 463.
explanation: Use DH = sum(bonds broken in reactants) - sum(bonds formed in products), counting every bond in the balanced equation. Reactants: ethene has 1 C=C and 4 C-H, and there are 3 O=O; bonds broken = 612 + 4(412) + 3(496) = 612 + 1648 + 1488 = 3748 kJ. Products: each CO2 has two C=O (4 total) and each H2O has two O-H (4 total); bonds formed = 4(805) + 4(463) = 3220 + 1852 = 5072 kJ. DH = 3748 - 5072 = -1324 kJ mol-1. The method inherently gives gaseous species, which is why H2O(g) is specified.

option_analysis.A: Wrong: computes (bonds formed) - (bonds broken). The correct expression is DH = (bonds broken) - (bonds formed); reversing it inverts the sign.
option_analysis.B: Wrong: breaks only 2 O=O bonds; the balanced equation requires 3 O2, so three O=O bonds are broken.
option_analysis.C: Wrong: counts only one O-H per water (2 in total). Each H2O has two O-H bonds, so 4 O-H bonds must be formed.
option_analysis.D: Wrong: counts only one C=O per CO2 (2 in total). Each CO2 contains two C=O bonds, so 4 C=O bonds must be formed.
option_analysis.E: Correct: bonds broken = C=C + 4 C-H + 3 O=O = 612 + 1648 + 1488 = 3748 kJ; bonds formed = 4 C=O + 4 O-H = 3220 + 1852 = 5072 kJ; DH = 3748 - 5072 = -1324 kJ mol-1.

author: mioitalia_editorial

subject: chemistry
subtopic: Ordering separation techniques for a three-component solid (sublimation, then dissolution/filtration, then crystallisation)
learning_objective: Design a correctly ordered separation scheme for a mixture of two water-soluble solids (one of which sublimes) and one insoluble solid, recognising that two water-soluble salts cannot be separated by cooling crystallisation alone.
question: A dry solid mixture contains three components: ammonium chloride (which sublimes on gentle heating and is soluble in water), sodium chloride (soluble in water, does not sublime) and silica sand (insoluble in water, does not sublime). A technician must recover all three components separately, each pure and dry. Which procedure achieves this?

choices.A: Heat gently to sublime the ammonium chloride onto a cold surface, then stir the residue with water and filter to obtain the sand as the residue, then evaporate the filtrate to crystallise the sodium chloride.
choices.B: Separate the three solids by fractional distillation, exploiting their different boiling points.
choices.C: Add water and filter off the sand, then cool the filtrate so that the ammonium chloride crystallises out, leaving the sodium chloride behind in solution.
choices.D: Add water and filter off the sand, then cool the filtrate strongly so that the sodium chloride crystallises out, and finally evaporate the remaining solution to recover the ammonium chloride.
choices.E: Heat gently to sublime the ammonium chloride onto a cold surface, then stir the residue with water and filter to obtain the sodium chloride as the residue, then evaporate the filtrate to recover the sand.

explanation: Only ammonium chloride sublimes, so gentle heating removes it first as a pure solid on a cold surface, leaving sodium chloride + sand. Stirring this residue with water dissolves the sodium chloride but not the sand, so filtration gives the sand as the (insoluble) residue and sodium chloride in the filtrate, which is then recovered by evaporating/crystallising the filtrate. All three are obtained pure. The key insight is that the two water-soluble salts (NH4Cl and NaCl) can only be separated from each other by exploiting the sublimation of ammonium chloride — not by dissolving them together and trying to crystallise one out selectively.

option_analysis.A: Correct: sublime the ammonium chloride first (pure), then dissolve and filter to obtain the sand as residue, then evaporate/crystallise the filtrate to recover the sodium chloride — all three components are obtained separately and pure.
option_analysis.B: Wrong: fractional distillation separates liquids of different boiling points; it is not a method for recovering three solids from a solid mixture.
option_analysis.C: Wrong: cooling the filtrate (which holds both soluble salts) does not leave pure sodium chloride in solution, because ammonium chloride is not fully removed and the sodium chloride is not recovered as a separate solid; the ammonium chloride is also not obtained pure.
option_analysis.D: Wrong: once the sand is filtered off, the filtrate contains BOTH ammonium chloride and sodium chloride, and cooling will not selectively crystallise sodium chloride — its solubility changes very little with temperature, whereas ammonium chloride's falls steeply, so the two soluble salts are not cleanly separated.
option_analysis.E: Wrong: the order/identities are muddled — after subliming the ammonium chloride and adding water, filtration gives the SAND (insoluble) as the residue and sodium chloride in the filtrate, not sodium chloride as the residue and sand in the filtrate.

author: mioitalia_editorial
